sentences.text: Key ideas
sentences.say: Key ideas

sentences.text: Squared error is a bad cost for logistic regression: with a sigmoid it gives a bumpy surface.
sentences.say: Squared error is a bad cost for logistic regression: with a sigmoid it gives a bumpy surface.

sentences.text: The right cost is the log loss.
sentences.say: The right cost is the log loss.

sentences.text: The log loss punishes a confident wrong answer very hard.
sentences.say: The log loss punishes a confident wrong answer very hard.

sentences.text: The gradient has exactly the same form as for linear regression: (prediction minus target) times the feature.
sentences.say: The gradient has exactly the same form as for linear regression: (prediction minus target) times the feature.

sentences.text: Only the prediction is now a sigmoid.
sentences.say: Only the prediction is now a sigmoid.

sentences.text: At w = 0 and b = 0 the cost is always 0.693, the natural log of 2.
sentences.say: At w equals 0 and b equals 0 the cost is always 0.693, the natural log of 2.

sentences.text: This is a quick bug check.
sentences.say: This is a quick bug check.

sentences.text: 10.1 Why not squared error?
sentences.say: 10.1 Why not squared error?

sentences.text: If you put the sigmoid inside the squared-error cost, the cost surface is no longer a single bowl: it has flat patches and traps, and gradient descent may get stuck.
sentences.say: If you put the sigmoid inside the squared-error cost, the cost surface is no longer a single bowl: it has flat patches and traps, and gradient descent may get stuck.

sentences.text: A different cost keeps the bowl shape (Ng, video 34).
sentences.say: A different cost keeps the bowl shape (Ng, video 34).

sentences.text: 10.2 The loss on one example
sentences.say: 10.2 The loss on one example

sentences.text: For one example with true label y and prediction f (a probability):
sentences.say: For one example with true label y and prediction f (a probability):

sentences.text: If y = 1, the loss is -log(f).
sentences.say: If y equals 1, the loss is -log(f).

sentences.text: When f is near 1 the loss is near 0.
sentences.say: When f is near 1 the loss is near 0.

sentences.text: When f is near 0 the loss explodes.
sentences.say: When f is near 0 the loss explodes.

sentences.text: If y = 0, the loss is -log(1 - f).
sentences.say: If y equals 0, the loss is -log(1 minus f).

sentences.text: The same, mirrored.
sentences.say: The same, mirrored.

sentences.text: The model is encouraged to be right, and to be humble when it is unsure.
sentences.say: The model is encouraged to be right, and to be humble when it is unsure.

sentences.text: Because y is either 0 or 1, the two cases fit in one line (Ng, video 35), and the cost J is the average of this loss over all m examples:

sentences.text: When y is 1 the second term vanishes, and when y is 0 the first does, which gives the two cases above.
sentences.say: When y is 1 the second term vanishes, and when y is 0 the first does, which gives the two cases above.

sentences.text: At w = 0 and b = 0 every prediction is 0.5, so every loss is -log(0.5) = 0.693, and so is the average.
sentences.say: At w equals 0 and b equals 0 every prediction is 0.5, so every loss is -log(0.5) equals 0.693, and so is the average.

sentences.text: If your code does not print 0.693 there, it has a bug.

sentences.text: 10.3 Where the log loss comes from
sentences.say: 10.3 Where the log loss comes from

sentences.text: Beyond the videos (StatQuest's Logistic Regression Details Pt 2 shows it step by step).
sentences.say: Beyond the videos (StatQuest's Logistic Regression Details Pt 2 shows it step by step).

sentences.text: The log loss is maximum likelihood in disguise.
sentences.say: The log loss is maximum likelihood in disguise.

sentences.text: The likelihood is the probability that the model assigned to exactly what happened: multiply f for every example with y = 1 and (1 - f) for every example with y = 0.
sentences.say: The likelihood is the probability that the model assigned to exactly what happened: multiply f for every example with y equals 1 and (1 minus f) for every example with y equals 0.

sentences.text: The best parameters make that product as large as possible.
sentences.say: The best parameters make that product as large as possible.

sentences.text: A product of many small numbers is awkward, so take the logarithm, which turns it into a sum, and flip the sign so that "largest likelihood" becomes "smallest cost".
sentences.say: A product of many small numbers is awkward, so take the logarithm, which turns it into a sum, and flip the sign so that "largest likelihood" becomes "smallest cost".

sentences.text: The result is the cost above.
sentences.say: The result is the cost above.

sentences.text: So it is not an arbitrary choice: it is the principle of making the observed data as probable as possible.
sentences.say: So it is not an arbitrary choice: it is the principle of making the observed data as probable as possible.
